Twined
TWYND
adj., v. (pp.)
From twine, to twist together, Old English twin, double thread. Webster 1828: twisted; convolved. In the Authorized Version the word appears almost exclusively in the phrase fine twined linen, the thread of the tabernacle: linen spun and doubled and twisted before it was ever woven.

Biblical Definition

Fine twined linen is the standing material of the sanctuary, and the adjective is doing real work. The thread is not simply fine; it has been twisted, doubled upon itself, so that what hangs in the court is strong as well as white. The curtains of the court on the south side were hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long (Exodus 27:9), and the whole enclosure the same: All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen (Exodus 38:16). The priests’ garments are cut from it — linen breeches of fine twined linen (Exodus 39:28) — and so are the inner curtains with their cherubim. Two things follow. First, the boundary between the camp and the holy place is made of the whitest and strongest thing Israel could produce, which is a sermon in cloth: what separates a sinner from God is purity, and purity is not flimsy. Second, God specified the thread. He did not merely command a fence; He named the fibre, the doubling, and the colours worked into it. The regulative principle of worship has a textile in the Old Testament: God says how, and not only that.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives TWINE as to twist; to wind or unite closely; and TWINED as twisted or convolved. The biblical phrase is exact: a thread twisted double before weaving, which is what makes fine linen both fine and strong.

expand to see more

TWINE, v.t. — To twist; to wind, as one thread around another. To unite closely; to embrace.

TWINED, pp. — Twisted; convolved; wound about.

The doubling is the whole force of the word. A single fine thread would be delicate; a fine thread twined is fine and durable together, which is precisely what a hanging exposed to weather and a garment worn in service both require.

Exodus 27:9 — "And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:"

Exodus 27:18 — "The length of the court shall be an hundred cubits, and the breadth fifty every where, and the height five cubits of fine twined linen, and their sockets of brass."

Exodus 38:16 — "All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen."

Exodus 39:28 — "And a mitre of fine linen, and goodly bonnets of fine linen, and linen breeches of fine twined linen,"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on fine twined linen is not redefinition but impatience — the modern habit of treating God’s specifications for worship as decorative detail rather than as command.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is contesting the meaning of twined thread. What is contested, constantly, is whether God’s stated particulars in worship are binding or merely illustrative. Chapters of Exodus specify the fibre, the twist, the colours, the cubits, and the sockets, and they specify them twice — once as command and once as compliance. That doubling in the text is not padding. It is the record that Israel did it as it was said.

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add. The tabernacle is the clearest case in Scripture of a God who cares about the how. When a congregation reasons that the details of worship are matters of taste because the tabernacle details seem small, it has drawn exactly the wrong conclusion from Exodus. The smallness of the detail is the proof of the seriousness of the claim.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is a passive participle meaning twisted, from a root for twisting or spinning, standing with the word for fine white linen. The phrase is fixed: fine linen, twisted.

expand to see more

Hebrew shazar (H7806) — to twist, to twine; the passive participle yields twined in the phrase fine twined linen.

Hebrew shesh (H8336) — fine white linen, byssus; the fibre itself (Exodus 27:9; Exodus 38:16).

The fixed phrase shesh moshzar occurs throughout Exodus 26-39 for the curtains, the hangings, the ephod, and the priestly breeches.

Later Hebrew uses buts for fine linen in Chronicles and Esther; the Exodus material keeps shesh.

Greek byssos renders the fibre in the Septuagint and stands behind the fine linen, clean and white of Revelation 19:8.

Usage

"Hangings for the court of fine twined linen (Exodus 27:9) — the boundary of the holy place is white and doubled."

"All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen (Exodus 38:16) — the command in chapter 27 and the compliance in chapter 38 are recorded word for word."

"Linen breeches of fine twined linen (Exodus 39:28) — the same thread that walls the court clothes the men who serve inside it."
